chain: Tape lifts or holds facial tissue
kinesiology-face-taping.text: Appearance-focused users apply elastic sports tape to the face in the hope of retraining facial muscles, holding tissue lifted and reducing puffiness for a more symmetrical look. The tape is studied for musculoskeletal use; facial use for appearance is untested.

chain: More balanced face at rest and in motion
facial-nerve-rehab-neurectomy.text: This is the medical route to a more symmetrical face when facial nerve paralysis has caused droop or uneven movement, using therapy, nerve repair, grafting or muscle transfers. It is an established clinical field for paralysis; use on normal faces for cosmetic symmetry is not a studied application.

chain: Claimed shifts in face and smile
tongue-tie-release.text: Some forum posters discuss releasing a tight lingual frenulum in the belief that better tongue posture improves facial symmetry and smile or tooth alignment. The procedure has feeding evidence in infants; the appearance claims are untested.

camera-angle-eye-dominance-selection.text: Users pick which side of the face and which angle to show, sometimes guided by eye dominance, so photos present the more flattering side. The change in how a photo looks is immediate. Faces are measurably asymmetric; a link between eye dominance and the best angle is not documented.

dental-midline-correction.text: People pursue midline correction through orthodontics so the line between the central incisors sits in line with the middle of the face, aiming for a more symmetrical smile. The midline concept is clearly defined; reviewed sources give no evidence on its effect on perceived appearance.

chain: Light it well, even out the smile
lighting-smiling-side-meta.text: Looksmaxxers use side choice, lighting direction and a deliberately even smile to make the face look more symmetrical and attractive on camera and in person. The visual change is immediate in the resulting photo. It is a popular photo tactic without direct research behind it.

chain: More masculine neck, jaw and frame
neck-training-flexion-extension.text: Users train the neck forward and back with towels, hands, plates or machines to build a thicker neck that they say complements the jaw, posture and physique. Neck training is well studied for pain and sport performance; its effect on appearance has not been studied.

neck-bridges-wrestler-bridges.text: Looksmaxxers borrow the wrestler's bridge from combat sports to thicken the neck for a stronger, more masculine look. The exercise is documented in wrestling, judo and MMA and is mainly described for back and glute strength; its use for neck appearance has no research.

chain: Front and side neck muscles grow
neck-curls-with-plate.text: Forum users perform loaded neck curls with a plate to thicken the neck and, by extension, give a more masculine frame, with some also claiming jaw and facial changes. The exercise is popular on forums; there are no trials on appearance outcomes.

shrugs-trap-training.text: Users train shrugs to build the upper trapezius, which fills the base of the neck and makes it look thicker. Sources reviewed cover muscle activation during the exercise, not its effect on how the neck looks.

isometric-neck-holds.text: Users press the head against a hand, band or wall to build neck size and definition, which proponents link to a stronger-looking jaw and neck. Isometric neck work is studied for pain and strength; its effect on appearance has not been studied.

platysmaplasty-neck-band-surgery.text: Platysmaplasty is chosen to remove visible vertical neck bands and sharpen the neck contour, usually alongside a neck lift or facelift. The contour change is visible after healing. Evidence comes from surgical case series rather than controlled trials.

chain: Neck skin, fat and muscle reshaped
cervicoplasty-cervical-contouring.text: Looksmaxxing communities list cervicoplasty among hardmaxxing procedures for a cleaner neck and jaw transition; in aesthetic surgery it is part of neck rejuvenation. The contour change is visible after healing. Evidence is documented in surgical series with little controlled data.

neck-liposuction.text: Neck liposuction is used to remove fat under the chin and along the neck, reducing a double chin and defining the jawline. The reduction in fullness is visible once swelling settles. Support comes from surgical case series; controlled trials are lacking.

neck-fillers-skin-boosters.text: Aesthetic-medicine users inject hyaluronic acid fillers and skin boosters to soften horizontal necklace lines and improve neck skin quality. Smoothing is visible after treatment. Only registered trials were found in reviewed sources, with no published results.

neck-cream-retinoid-for-necklines.text: Skincare-oriented users apply neck creams, some containing retinoids, to improve lines, laxity, crepiness and pigmentation on the neck and decolletage. Small product-specific studies report improvement in skin signs.

tech-neck-correction.text: Users apply exercises and ergonomic habits to undo forward head posture from screen use, which is said to shorten the visual neck and soften the jaw-to-neck transition. Symptoms of tech neck are studied; appearance effects of correcting it are not.

neck-stretches-chin-tucks.text: Users do chin tucks and neck stretches, sometimes adding weighted curls, to improve neck posture and, per forum claims, lift the hyoid area for a sharper profile. Chin tucks are used in physical therapy for neck complaints; appearance effects are unstudied.

sternocleidomastoid-scm-hypertrophy.text: Looksmaxxers aim to build the sternocleidomastoid, the large muscle on each side of the neck, so the neck looks thicker and more defined. The muscle's anatomy is well described; deliberate hypertrophy for appearance has not been studied.

neck-to-jaw-angle-cervicomental-angle-th.text: Forum frameworks hold that a cervicomental angle of roughly 105 to 120 degrees reads as more attractive in profile. Surgical literature describes the angle and how it changes with aging, but no study supports the specific range as a measure of attractiveness.

collar-and-shirt-choice-for-thick-neck.text: People with thick necks select collar shapes such as spread, point, button-down or mandarin and a suitable shirt fit to show the neck to its best effect. The change in look is immediate when worn. Collar types are documented; their effects on appearance have not been studied.

fat-loss-to-reveal-neck.text: Users cut body fat to show sharper neck and jaw contours and reduce a double chin where excess fat is the cause. Where a double chin comes from bone structure rather than fat, sources note it usually needs surgical correction.

whey-creatine-bulking-for-neck.text: Looksmaxxers pair a calorie surplus, whey protein and creatine with direct neck exercises to add neck size and a stronger-looking frame and jaw area. The supplements are studied for muscle gain in general, not specifically for the neck.

chain: Stone scraped along neck and jaw
gua-sha-neck-lymphatic-drainage.text: Popularized on social media in 2021 and 2022, gua sha on the jaw and neck is used for debloating, a sharper jawline and skin rejuvenation. The tool-and-oil technique comes from traditional Chinese medicine; clinical evidence for these appearance aims is lacking.

chain: Fat cells under chin broken down
Slimmer chin, neck and jowl line
kybella-for-neck-jowl.text: Kybella is injected to reduce fat under the chin for a slimmer, more defined chin and neck, with jowl and neck use being off-label. The reduction is visible after treatment. It was FDA-approved in 2015 for submental fat.

chain: Look of buzzed hair or density
scalp-micropigmentation.text: Scalp micropigmentation is used to give a bald or thinning scalp the look of a close buzz cut or greater density, and to conceal transplant and other scalp scars. The visual effect is immediate; it camouflages rather than regrows hair.

prp-for-hair.text: Users get scalp injections of their own platelet-rich plasma for androgenetic alopecia or alopecia areata, as an option alongside or instead of minoxidil or finasteride. Small trials report gains, but the research base is limited and protocols vary.

exosome-hair-therapy.text: Clinics and cosmetic brands offer exosome serums, microneedling and injections said to prompt dormant follicles to regrow hair. Only small registered trials exist so far, so the regrowth claim remains largely untested.

stem-cell-hair-therapy.text: Clinic treatments inject fat-derived, follicle-derived or donor cells, or cell-derived extracts, into the scalp to slow hair loss or promote regrowth. Small trials are registered and no approved product exists.

hair-cloning.text: Hair cloning is a long-promised approach in which follicle cells are multiplied in the laboratory and implanted, aiming to remove the donor-supply limit of hair transplants. It remains in animal and lab research rather than clinical use.
